title: Next.js routing, taken apart
dek: Next.js 16.4 turns an app/ folder tree into a sorted route table, one server entry per URL, prerendered segment files and per-segment prefetch hints, all before the first request. This teardown follows one route, app/sec0/a/[id]/page.tsx, from file to click through the code at v16.4.0, and prices each precomputation with numbers measured on a 2-vCPU machine. It ends with the practices that moved those numbers, and the beliefs the code contradicts.
byline: 14 October 2026 · Subject: vercel/next.js@v16.4.0 (e273d5b2e869), released 6 October 2026 · Read from the source, the docs at the tag and the release posts; timings measured on this machine
description: A teardown of Next.js 16.4 folder routing: file grammar, build, request path, rendering, caching, client router and prefetch, with measured costs.
og_description: Next.js routing read end to end at v16.4.0 (commit e273d5b2): how the app/ tree becomes a route table, a LoaderTree and prerendered segment files; how next start resolves a request; how segments render, cache and prefetch; and what each precomputation costs, measured on a 2-vCPU machine, with the practices that changed the numbers.

sections.title: One rule, many precomputations
figures: fig-golden-trace · backbone strip (SVG, wide) · one route from file to click in fifteen boxes across three lanes (BUILD, SERVER, BROWSER), each box showing the real bytes of one artifact and each arrow its writer and reader function · data: gap-golden-trace walk-through steps 1-15 and its artifact table; FIG-6; H17, H26-H28, H38
sections.brief:
Thesis. The App Router's grammar is one rule: folders name URL segments, a closed set of file stems gives each segment its behaviour, and everything else in app/ is invisible to routing (DOSSIER §1.1; N12, N1135). Because the structure is declared in files, `next build` can enumerate routes, compile one entry per URL, sort a route table, prerender the static parts, split client code per segment and record per-segment prefetch hints before any request arrives. The server and the browser then read those artifacts instead of rediscovering structure. Every efficiency follows from that, and so does every cost. Short framing section: lede plus four or five paragraphs and the figure.

Say what the reader can do after reading: read a .next/ directory and know which function wrote each file; predict what a visible link, a click, a cookies() call, a "use client" placement or a proxy.ts costs; and pick settings (experimental.cpus, the build cache, prefetchInlining, cacheComponents plus partialPrefetching, a Proxy matcher) knowing their measured effect here.

Subject: next@16.4.0, tag v16.4.0, commit e273d5b2e869d0be06c0e86f788e1594f9dd40cf, released 6 October 2026 per nextjs.org/blog/next-16-4 (V3, C14). Method: code at the tag; docs/ at the tag; release posts; a lab on this machine (DOSSIER §4.1 Machine row). Introduce the running example and /dyn (writer_notes). State the price side up front with four measured numbers, each with its script, and leave the explanations to later sections: rendered output ships twice on a hard load (E2: leaf "use client" placement made RSC 5.6x and HTML 2.3x larger than layout-top, lab:scripts/e2-boundary.mjs, H15); every visible link costs two requests (12-link page: 24 requests, 60,768 B decoded, 20,143 B on the wire, e3-nav.mjs, H20); the build cache does not skip prerendering (static generation about 24 s at N=400 cold, warm and after an edit, build-bench.mjs, H9); a no-op proxy.ts adds +0.93 ms p50 per matched request (+39% on a static page, e4-latency.mjs, H32). sections.title: What a folder means
figures: fig-folder-tree · annotated tree (SVG, wide) · one app/ tree; beside each file its served URL or why it is not routable, colour-coded by rule (group, private, slot, dynamic, catch-all, optional catch-all, interception, metadata with hash suffix, route handler, %5F); root files proxy.ts and instrumentation.ts; inset: the same tree under pages/, where every file is a route · data: conventions.md § Figure ideas 1; FIG-1; N6-N12, N55, N60, N71, N93, N95, N101-N106, N111, N116
sections.brief:
Thesis. Discovery keeps four kinds of file; everything else in app/ is invisible. Many file paths collapse onto one URL, groups and slots vanish before the route table exists so they cost nothing per request, and 16.4's strict route matching turns three structural mistakes into build errors.

What is discovered. collectAppFiles walks app/ and keeps page/route files plus metadata files, the root not-found, layout and default (N6; build/route-discovery.ts:101-131; server/lib/find-page-file.ts:100-106). template, loading, error and the access fallbacks are never discovered; they are looked up per segment when a page's tree is assembled, so they cannot create routes (N7; build/webpack/loaders/next-app-loader/index.ts:73-92). Turbopack classifies by stem against a closed list of twelve (N15; crates/next-core/src/app_structure.rs:377-395). pageExtensions defaults to ['tsx','ts','jsx','js'] (server/config-shared.ts:2308), so page.ts works although the docs' tables omit it (N13, N14; docs project-structure.mdx § Routing Files).

Colocation and private folders. A folder is routable only with page or route (N12; docs § Colocation). In next build, `_folder` is filtered on the directory entry before descent, so it is never read (N8; lib/recursive-readdir.ts:81-86); next dev still reads and watches it (server/lib/router-utils/setup-dev-bundler.ts:402-417). %5F spells a literal underscore (N11). Pages contrast in one sentence: every page-extension file under pages/ is a route, with no `_` pruning (N975). The 2.5-5x discovery-walk ratio belongs to §12; mention it only as a pointer.

Path to URL. Excerpt X1: normalizeAppPath, shared/lib/router/utils/app-paths.ts:23-52 (comments trimmed to fit 25 lines). It deletes (group), every @slot and a trailing page/route, and nothing else (N55). Interception markers survive; metadata renaming happens elsewhere (/robots -> /robots.txt/route; a hash suffix for files under groups or slots: N103, N104). getSegmentParam maps [x], [...x], [[...x]] to dynamic, catchall, optional-catchall (N60); on the wire there are 11 short codes such as d, c, oc, di(..) (N61).

Slots and interception. @folder is a named slot passed to the parent layout; children is implicit (N71). Every slot renders on the server even when the layout hides it (N74; parallel-routes.mdx § Conditional Routes). The docs give three answers for a missing default.js and the code shows all three can happen (N76, N78, N79). Interception markers resolve against route segments (N93) and compile to a beforeFiles rewrite that fires only when the next-url header matches (N95; lib/generate-interception-routes-rewrites.ts:9-60); a refresh renders the canonical page (N97).

Strict route matching. Excerpt X8: server/config.ts:460-468 (strictRouteMatching = !deprecated.looseRouteMatching; forced off when explicitParallelRouteChildren is false). Three new build errors (incompatible slots, interception without a canonical page, unmatched pages: N82; build/entries.ts:436-526) and pruned catch-all matchers (N83). The opt-out appears nowhere in docs/ or errors/ (N81); PR #97397, merged 2026-09-21; the release post is silent (N85, N1123).

Root conventions. proxy.ts is detected only beside app/ (N111) and is not a rename: it always compiles for Node.js, while middleware.ts still targets edge unless it sets nodejs (N112; build/entries.ts:339-352). Without a matcher it runs on every request because the default matcher is /:path* (N116; entries.ts:603-607); its cost is §05's. Typed routes come from the same discovery (N128-N130).

Owned elsewhere: per-segment boundary stack and what error/loading catch (§06); validateAppPaths and the /[a]/x conflict (§03); sorting and regexes (§04); root-layout MPA navigation (§08).

sections.title: From folders to entries
figures: fig-build-pipeline · swimlane (SVG, wide) · lanes: JS orchestrator (discover-routes -> generate-route-types -> generate-routes-manifest -> compile -> static-check -> static-generation -> write-route-bundle-stats, each with the artifact it writes), Turbopack (get_directory_tree memoised per directory -> walk_tree -> one server file per page, per-page manifests merged), webpack (server -> edge -> client, client entries injected by the server compile); marks 'tree read twice', the clean keep-list, where validateAppPaths runs (build) and where getSortedRoutes runs (next start); annotated with the N=400 Turbopack cold QUIET phase medians · data: FIG-2; N146, N154, N156, N162, N185, N142, N195, N198, N233; lab/results/summary-builds.csv
sections.brief:
Thesis. next build is a fixed sequence of traced phases that turns the tree into entries before anything is compiled. Under Turbopack the tree is read twice. Validation rejects whole-path ambiguity but misses per-level slug conflicts, which crash next start. The prerender pool is sized from the host's CPUs, not the container's.

Which compiler. With no flag, next build defaults to Turbopack and records TURBOPACK=auto; --webpack opts out (N146; lib/bundler.ts:99-103). A defaulted Turbopack build that finds a webpack() function and no turbopack key exits instead of ignoring it (N150; lib/turbopack-warning.ts:146-166). The webpack loader's own comment calls Turbopack "the canonical implementation going forward" (N153; next-app-loader/index.ts:1047-1054).

Phases. build() is a sequence of traced spans: discover-routes -> generate-route-types -> generate-routes-manifest -> compile -> static-check -> static-generation -> write-route-bundle-stats (N154; build/index.ts:1336-4843). The routes manifest is computed from discovery before compilation (N162). The clean step keeps cache/, dev/, diagnostics/, lock and trace, which is what keeps caches warm (N156; build/index.ts:1379-1388). In a Turbopack build the tree is read by JS discoverRoutes and again by Rust get_directory_tree, a memoised turbo-task per directory (N185 is a reconstruction from both call sites: badge it so; N142; crates/next-core/src/app_structure.rs:331-343).

Validation and its gap. validateAppPaths rejects syntax errors, semantic errors and ambiguity by erasing param names: /blog/[id] and /blog/[slug] collide, /[category]/posts and /posts/[slug] pass (N189, N190; build/validate-app-paths.ts:16-139, 155-186); its own comment says it duplicates the older trie (N191). It does not check per-level slug consistency. Measured: app/[a]/x plus app/[b]/y built with exit 0; next start printed Ready and exited 1 after 509-843 ms (H39, N1280; lab:scripts/e8-sortconflict.mjs). Excerpt X68: shared/lib/router/utils/sorted-routes.ts:121-134, the deprecated sorter still used at boot (server/lib/router-utils/filesystem.ts:134; N241).

Entries. webpack: one server entry per page named app/<key> (N195; build/entries.ts:561-568); App pages get no initial client entry, the server compile discovers client components and injects their entries (N198, N164; build/webpack-build/impl.ts:267-285). Turbopack writes one server file per page (N233; crates/next-api/src/app.rs:2066-2083). Both wrap each layout and page in a lazy getter; under webpack's eager mode that defers evaluation, not bundling (N215).

Static reads. Segment config passes a regex gate, then a 500-entry SHA-1-keyed SWC cache, and only literal export const values count (N269-N271). generateStaticParams cascades top-down, one call per parent combination, sequentially (N282; build/static-paths/app.ts:724-823).

Workers. Default experimental.cpus is max(1, os.cpus().length - 1) (config-shared.ts:2422-2426; it also reads CIRCLE_NODE_TOTAL), capped at tasks + 1 (N1138; build/index.ts:979-1004), with at most 8 renders per worker and at least 25 pages per worker (N1250). Measured: 7 workers inside the 2-CPU cgroup (H1). State the trap here; the fix and its effect are §12's.

Cost at a glance (H4-H6, build-bench.mjs): cold wall Turbopack 27.6 / 38.6 s at 21 / 101 routes and 70.4 s at 401 (QUIET rerun; 97.5 s contended) vs webpack 52.2 / 69.3 / 134.3 s (QUIET at 401); CPU ratio 1.60-1.63x; marginal 0.20 CPU-s per route (Turbopack) vs 0.31-0.33 (webpack).

Figure: annotate N=400 Turbopack cold QUIET medians: compile 25.2 s, TypeScript 13.8 s, static generation 21.7 s, wall 70.4 s; phase spans overlap, so do not draw them as a partition.

Owned elsewhere: manifest contents and the LoaderTree (§04); cache, cpus and prerender-count practices (§12); per-route client splitting (§10).

sections.title: The route table, the LoaderTree and the manifests
figures: fig-loader-tree · nested boxes (SVG) · the compiled 4-tuple literal for /sec0/a/[id] (X43): '' -> sec0 -> a -> [id] -> __PAGE__, each node drawn as [segment, slots, modules, staticSiblings], root modules layout/not-found/forbidden/unauthorized/global-error, the page getter instrumentModuleGetter(() => a.r(79741)), slot 4 '[]' (known none, Turbopack) vs 'null' (unknown, webpack dev); inset: a /dashboard tree with an @analytics slot showing (__SLOT__) and __DEFAULT__ · data: FIG-3; X43, X18; N88, N204, N212, N1257, N1266-N1268
sections.brief:
Thesis. The build's output is a set of data structures the server and client read instead of the folder tree: a specificity-sorted table of anchored regexes, one LoaderTree literal per URL, a prerender manifest that classifies every URL, six files per prerendered URL and a per-segment hint tree.

The table. generateRoutesManifest sorts every page with sortPages: static segment 0, [x] 1, [...x] 2, [[...x]] 3, compared left to right, a path that ends first wins a tie, then localeCompare (N237-N239; shared/lib/router/utils/sortable-routes.ts:20-58, 75-114; build/generate-routes-manifest.ts:69-95). The older trie sorter is @deprecated but still used at runtime (N240, N241). Sorting 1,000 routes took 14-26 ms (N244). Each dynamic route gets an anchored regex with nxtP-prefixed named groups (N246, N247; shared/lib/router/utils/route-regex.ts:120, 163-171). Show the example's row as a <pre> (lab:apps/scale-N400/.next/routes-manifest.json): "regex": "^/sec0/a/([^/]+?)(?:/)?$", "namedRegex": "^/sec0/a/(?<nxtPid>[^/]+?)(?:/)?$", "routeKeys": {"nxtPid":"nxtPid"}; it is the 3rd of 119 dynamic routes beside 285 static ones (N1260, N1262). The split is by URL shape, not render mode: the per-request cookies() page /dyn is a static route (DOSSIER §1.4). The manifest's rsc block fixes the wire contract: the Vary value rsc, next-router-state-tree, next-router-prefetch, next-router-segment-prefetch and the .rsc and .segments/<path>.segment.rsc suffixes (N256, N1263; generate-routes-manifest.ts:121-136).

The LoaderTree. Excerpt X18: server/lib/app-dir-module.ts:7-29, the 4-tuple type whose doc comment explains staticSiblings (verbatim, 23 lines). Walk the compiled literal in Figure {{fig-loader-tree}}: the root node carries layout, not-found, forbidden, unauthorized and global-error; every node ends in []; Turbopack writes [] for "known to have no static siblings" and the field is null (unknown) in webpack dev (N212, N1267; crates/next-core/src/app_page_loader_tree.rs:328-442). The 4th element reaches the client only when experimental.optimisticRouting is on, the 16.4 default (N1268; server/app-render/app-render.tsx:535-551; config-shared.ts:2411). Slots appear as virtual (__SLOT__) levels and a synthesized fallback as __DEFAULT__ (N88).

The manifests. server/app-paths-manifest.json maps 405 keys to server files, merged from per-page fragments (N1258). app-path-routes-manifest.json maps keys to URLs from what the compiler emitted (N257, N258). prerender-manifest.json (version 4): 754 routes and 118 dynamic patterns; /sec0/a/1 is complete/static with initialRevalidateSeconds false; the pattern row has fallback null -> blocking (N1264, N1265); at N=400 it is 647,564 B, about 859 B per route (N1167). There is no app-build-manifest.json at 16.4 (N255). route-bundle-stats.json replaces the removed First Load JS column (N288); prefetch-hints.json is §09's.

Six files per URL (H17, N1271; export/routes/app-page.ts:181-254): 1.html 9,954 B; 1.rsc 5,866; 1.meta 1,036; 1.segments/_tree 275; _full 5,866 (byte-identical to 1.rsc); sec0/a/$d$id/__PAGE__ 4,942. Segment files are re-encoded from the page's RSC buffer, not re-rendered (N441; server/app-render/collect-segment-data.tsx:157-175, 319-326). 1.meta replays headers: x-nextjs-stale-time 300, six implicit tags _N_T_/layout to _N_T_/sec0/a/1, and a routeCache.key (N1273). Layouts repeat per id: 1.rsc and 2.rsc differ in 3 of 25 lines (N1278). Totals at N=400: 756 HTML, 754 RSC, 2,268 segment files, no layout files because of inlining (H16).

Owned elsewhere: how the server uses the table per request (§05); hint bits and inlining (§09); first-load JS (§10); soft-tag invalidation (§07).

sections.title: The request path in next start

sections.brief:
Thesis. next start is one process that turns manifests into Sets and a sorted regex list at boot and never reads app/ again. Routing costs microseconds. The request-time costs sit elsewhere: the first request after boot, promoting build seeds, and Proxy.

Boot. One process: the render server is required in-process, with no IPC (N314; server/lib/router-server.ts:355-357). setupFsCheck builds the inventory only from manifests (N327); public/, static/ and .next/static/ become Sets (N326); one regex matcher per dynamic route, ordered by getSortedRoutes (N329; server/lib/router-utils/filesystem.ts:102-135, 509-526). Page bodies still come from the file-system IncrementalCache behind a 50 MB LRU (C12).

Resolution. Excerpt X51: server/lib/router-utils/resolve-routes.ts:85-117, the phase list (comments trimmed to 25 lines), built once in production (N344). check_fs is Set.has over six sets behind an 8 MiB LRU that also caches misses, so a public/ file shadows an app page (N331, N333; filesystem.ts:175-213, 757-764). Dynamic routes are tried only inside checkTrue, a linear first-match scan (N350). /sec0/a/1 misses check_fs because appFiles holds patterns and matches 3rd (N1281). Measured (e6-match.mjs, H34): 5.8 us per hit and 8.0 us per miss at 100 dynamic routes; 85 and 168 us at 1,000; 9.7x the matchers cost 14.6x the time; static lookups under 0.1 us; a rerun moved absolute times by up to 30%. At 1,000 patterns matching stays under 0.2 ms against a 2.37 ms static TTFB (N1246).

Hand-off and cache. The match travels to BaseServer as request meta (N377); 16.4 deleted the server route-matcher stack (PR #94157, 2026-08-15; N378). Vary is the four router headers, plus next-url only for interceptable paths (N384). _rsc is the first 96 bits of SHA-256 over those headers, not the URL; a mismatch gets a 307 (N1291, N385); all twelve /_tree prefetches used nVRY9RLVAUtqyrUj (N1292). Only SSG requests that need no dynamic response get a cache key; dynamic pages get null, so they are neither cached nor coalesced (N397, N450; build/templates/app-page-runtime.ts:677-695).

New in 16.4: seeds. The key is /route-cache/<kind>/<sha256(module)>/$<path>; the first request copies the build's files and writes .html last (N1286; server/lib/route-cache-key.ts:87-113). About 12 ms once per path: 15.7-17.2 vs 3.95-4.24 ms medians (H38, e8-seed-promotion.mjs). x-nextjs-prerender is sent twice, a setHeader plus an appendHeader of the stored .meta (N1283).

First request. preloadEntriesOnStart (default on) loads all 405 entries in the background: first request 1.24 s median, 394 ms with it off, 146 ms after 4 s idle; 0.89-1.05 s CPU in unstable_preloadEntries (H37, N1289, N1290; e8-cold-prof.mjs, e8-preload-tradeoff.mjs). Warm TTFB p50/p95 (H31, e4-latency.mjs): static 2.37/3.67 ms; SSG param 2.63/4.16; route handler 2.26/3.76; cookies() 5.55/9.84; static through a no-op Proxy 3.30/5.35.

Proxy. Matchers are widened at build time to _next/data, .rsc and .segments forms (N363) and end-anchored, so '/about' does not match /about/team, against the docs (N364). A RegExp per try costs under 1 us (C5). The cost: +0.93 ms p50 (+39%); LOCKED +0.909 ms TTFB and +888 us CPU per matched request (H32). A matched request re-enters handleRequest (N368); excerpt X65: server/next-server.ts:2006-2010, the thrown BubbledError (69 us by itself). Unmatched requests still paid 40-45 us (N1310; base-server.ts:740-748).

fig-proxy-cost bars (H33, us/request; per-bucket medians of three rounds, which do not sum to the 888 us total; say so): Proxy bundle 437, plumbing 242, router layer 85, second BaseServer pass 72, unattributed ~102, GC 25; call out BubbledError 69 and require()/path/fs 69.

sections.brief:
Thesis. A route renders as a fixed per-segment stack of boundaries derived from the folder tree. An HTML request renders the whole tree and ships its output twice. A soft navigation renders from the first differing segment, but only for dynamic targets: there are three cases, not one (C3).

The render. An HTML request builds the full tree from the root (N412). createComponentTree resolves each segment's template, error and loading modules, lazily loads its layout or page, and builds child slots concurrently with Promise.all, so siblings never wait for each other (N413, N875; server/app-render/create-component-tree.tsx:191-260, 527-722).

The stack. The client wraps each slot in TemplateContext.Provider (keyed by the state key) > ScrollHandler > ErrorBoundary > LoadingBoundary > HTTPAccessFallbackBoundary > RedirectBoundary > child (N417; client/components/layout-router.tsx:666-729). The segment's own layout renders the LayoutRouter for each of its slots and passes in that segment's error, template and fallbacks (N20; create-component-tree.tsx:696-724). Hence error.js cannot catch the layout beside it, and loading.js cannot cover data read in the sibling layout (N29; docs loading.mdx § Instant Loading States). The server emits no Suspense for loading.tsx: LoadingBoundaryProvider puts it in context and the client wraps each child slot (N416). loading is stored on the parent's data, which the code calls "an implementation accident" (N23; layout-router.tsx:673-686). The browser template key is name|value|type, so a new param value remounts and search params never do (N28, N644).

Payload twice. The Flight stream is rendered once and teed: one branch feeds Fizz SSR, the other is inlined as self.__next_f.push scripts (N430, N431; app-render.tsx:4069-4081, 4207-4266). The example document had exactly two pushes, the second carrying all 5,866 B of 1.rsc (N1284); HTML was 1.47-1.73x its decoded RSC payload (N1210). Responses are trees of transport nodes {s, h, d: {r, p, v}, c}, c a Map keyed by slot name, new in 16.4 (PR #96439; N420, N421).

Partial rendering. Excerpt X73: server/app-render/walk-tree-with-flight-router-state.tsx:143-154, the four conditions under which a level renders (no client state, segment or param changed, page search changed, 'refetch'). A level the client already has comes back skipped, {r: null, p: true, v: null}: its layout is not rendered, but its module is still imported to compute prefetch hints and its metadata is still resolved (N426; shared/lib/rsc-transport.ts:213-215; lib/metadata/resolve-metadata.ts:85-86, 135-136).

Three cases (H26-H28). (a) Prefetched static target: the click sends nothing; /sec0/a/1 -> /sec0/a/2 finished in 50 ms (N1297). (b) Unprefetched prerendered target: the handler deletes the Flight headers of a non-dynamic RSC request to an SSG page (build/templates/app-page-runtime.ts:521-532, 724-732), so it returns the whole cached .rsc: 5,866 B decoded, 1,619 B wire; with or without the state tree the bytes were identical, 5,948 B, a cache HIT (N1212, N1299); the file-system cache reads the page as one entry, with a TODO for per-segment entries (N1218). (c) Dynamic target: /sec0/a/2 -> /dyn returned 2,602 B against 4,433 B without the state tree (-41%); a dynamic sibling under two shared layouts went from 5,894 to 2,857 B (-52%) (N1213-N1215). In every case the client keeps shared CacheNodes; the <html> and sec0 <section> DOM nodes survived even case (b) (N1297). "Not refetched and not remounted" is guaranteed; "not re-rendered" is not, and was not measured (V4; §08 quotes the TODO).

Owned elsewhere: holes and shells (§07); the client diff code (§08); prefetching (§09); "use client" placement as a practice (§13).

sections.title: Static shells and dynamic holes
figures: fig-shell-and-holes · mechanism diagram plus timeline (SVG, wide) · left: one layout -> page tree drawn twice (legacy: cookies() throws, revalidate 0, whole route private/no-store; Cache Components: the call hangs and only the nearest Suspense or loading.tsx becomes a hole with its fallback in the shell); middle: the two-pass prerender (prospective fill into the Resume Data Cache, then the final pass advancing ShellStatic -> PrefetchStatic -> NavigationStatic -> Static, pending after the last task = hole); right: the PPR response timeline (2,298-B shell at about 4.5 ms, resumed part later, private no-store, x-nextjs-postponed: 1); inset: cacheLife placement thresholds as a 2-D chart (stale < 30 s out of every prerender; stale < 300 s out of the App Shell; expire < 300 s or revalidate 0 out of static shells) · data: FIG-11; X79, X84; N482-N505, N546-N548, N607; H35; lab:scripts/e7-latency.mjs, e7-ppr-body.mjs
sections.brief:
Thesis. Two rendering models differ in what one request API costs. In the legacy model a cookies() call makes the whole route dynamic; under Cache Components it makes one hole, and the folder tree supplies the Suspense boundaries that make holes legal. PPR then brings a dynamic page's first byte near a static page's, and pays in total time, bytes and CDN cacheability.

The switch. cacheComponents is false in the framework defaults; create-next-app writes cacheComponents: true and partialPrefetching: true (N466, N1120; config-shared.ts:2345). The 16.4 post recommends it for every app and says it becomes the default in Next.js 17 (N1119).

Two models, one API. Excerpt X79: server/request/cookies.ts:75-90 (verbatim; it shows both branches). In a 'prerender' store the call returns a promise that never resolves (N482; server/dynamic-rendering-utils.ts:72-95). In 'prerender-legacy' it calls throwToInterruptStaticGeneration, which sets revalidate = 0 and throws DynamicServerError, so the route goes dynamic (N887; server/app-render/dynamic-rendering.ts:244-260). Hanging promises are typed by data kind: cookies/headers may resolve in a runtime shell; known params resolve at PrefetchStatic and stay out of the App Shell; searchParams only at PrefetchRuntime; connection() and uncached fetch never (N483, N484, N489; server/app-render/staged-rendering.ts:4-42).

The two-pass prerender. Pass 1 renders with a CacheSignal and fills every "use cache" entry into a per-page Resume Data Cache; pass 2 replays and advances one stage per task; anything still pending after the last task is a hole (N498-N501; app-render.tsx:9136-9148, 9684-9797). A hole is legal only if a Suspense frame sits above it in the component stack; otherwise the build fails with a blocking-route error (N503; dynamic-rendering.ts:748-800). Every loading.tsx is a Suspense at a folder edge (N505; client/components/layout-router.tsx:479-494).

Lifetimes decide placement. Excerpt X84: server/use-cache/constants.ts:3-5 (MIN_PRERENDERABLE_EXPIRE 300, MIN_PREFETCHABLE_STALE 30, MIN_SHELL_STALE 300) with their meaning (N546-N548). Lifetimes flow upward as a minimum, tags as a union (N527). The collected stale reaches the client as x-nextjs-stale-time or in-band, floored at 30 s (N512, N513).

What the tree lets the build emit. A base-route shell for every dynamic pattern plus one per known-param prefix (N583; build/static-paths/app.ts:1297-1370). Lab v3 (N=20, e7-build.mjs, H36): 41 HTML files instead of 35 (the PPR shell dyn.html and five base-route shells such as sec0/a/[id].html); route table ○17 ●13 ƒ4 -> ○27 ◐8; build CPU 34.52 vs 33.70 CPU-s, within run-to-run spread. Invalidation follows the tree: every render carries soft tags _N_T_/layout down to .../page, and revalidatePath is revalidateTag on one of them (N567, N569; server/lib/implicit-tags.ts:26-57); app/shop/[category]/[product]/page.tsx gets five (N568).

PPR on the wire. next start sends the cached shell plus a resumed render in one response marked Cache-Control: private, no-cache, no-store, max-age=0, must-revalidate (N607; build/templates/app-page-runtime.ts:2377-2388). Measured (H35, LOCKED, pooled n=900): TTFB p50 3.63 ms vs 6.45 ms for the same cookies()-in-Suspense page without Cache Components, close to static 3.07 ms; total 15.35 vs 7.92 ms; 14,360 vs 7,671 B decoded; the 2,298-B shell arrived at about 4.5 ms; x-nextjs-postponed: 1.

Per process. ResponseCache and IncrementalCache stay per-process without a handler; the default "use cache" handler is a 50 MB LRU serving as both default and remote, and in production it drops entries once past revalidate (N552-N554). One sentence on the legacy per-segment revalidate: the render-time minimum reaches the manifest, read in code without a build (V1, C9).

Owned elsewhere: Partial Prefetching and App Shells on the client (§09); adopting Cache Components and multi-instance handlers as practices (§13).

sections.title: The client router and the Segment Cache
figures: fig-segment-cache-keys · diagram (SVG) · top: the route cache key {pathname, search, nextUrl} with nextUrl collapsed to Fallback unless the response varied on Next-Url; middle: the per-segment vary-path trie (request key /sec0/a/$d$id/__PAGE__ or a group key !KG1hcmtldGluZyk -> search slot for pages only -> params nearest first), unread params re-keyed to Fallback, and the App Shell path with every non-root param Fallback; bottom: old vs new render tree during /sec0/a/1 -> /sec0/a/2 with reused CacheNodes greyed and the one new __PAGE__ node · data: FIG-8 (cache-key half); X105; N640-N643, N662, N697-N704, N709, N1194, N1276
sections.brief:
Thesis. The browser holds a serializable state tree and a render tree and diffs them copy-on-write. Segment identity is structural, by names and types, never values, which is what lets one cache entry serve many URLs. The client learns the route map from responses instead of downloading it.

State. FlightRouterState is a positional tuple: segment, children map, refresh state, refresh marker, prefetch-hints bitmask, rendered search; it is written into history.state (N634, N781; shared/lib/app-router-types.ts:143-183; client/components/app-router.tsx:128-153). Beside it sits a render tree of CacheNodes carrying rsc and prefetchRsc (N637). Router state lives outside React and is fed in through use() (N652); prefetching never dispatches an action, it writes into a global cache (N654).

Keys. A segment's request key encodes position and param names and types: [id] travels as $d$id, a route group as ! plus base64url (N640, N1194, N1276; shared/lib/segment-cache/segment-value-encoding.ts:13-35, 62-75). All five ids therefore share /sec0/a/$d$id/__PAGE__.

The diff. startPPRNavigation builds the next render tree synchronously (N661; client/components/render-tree.ts:206-296). Excerpt X105: client/components/render-tree.ts:513-522, the reuse branch with its TODO about React bail-out (verbatim, about 10 lines) (N662, V4). New segments are filled from the BFCache, then the Segment Cache, else given a deferred promise (N669). Missing data goes into one request whose tree marks the top-most needing segment of each branch 'refetch'; if nothing is missing, no request is sent (N671, N672). navigate() returns synchronously when the tree is cached (N655).

Root layouts. A change of root layout returns null and forces a full page load; identity is structural, so /en -> /fr under app/[lang]/layout.tsx stays soft (N51, N664; client/components/router-reducer/is-navigating-to-new-root-layout.ts:4-69). Other MPA fallbacks: a non-RSC response, a build or deployment ID mismatch (N675).

The Segment Cache. Two global maps behind one 50 MB LRU that cannot be configured (N697, N707, N909). Route entries are keyed {pathname, search, nextUrl}; nextUrl becomes a wildcard unless the response varied on Next-Url (N698, N699). Segment entries are keyed by a vary path: request key, then search (pages only), then params nearest first (N700, N643); with varyParams (default on) unread params are re-keyed to Fallback (N702; segment-cache/vary-path.ts:411-439). Stale time comes from the server, floored at 30 s; staleTimes.static (300 s) is only the fallback (N709, N910). Measured: documents carried x-nextjs-stale-time: 300; 0 of 1,775 tree and segment responses carried it, because the value travels in-band as an iterable yielding 300 (N1346; e7-nav.mjs).

Slots, interception, history. On a soft navigation an unmatched slot keeps its active segment (N786). Interception depends on Next-Url, computed from the changed part of the tree (N791); router.refresh() replays the previous Next-Url (N794; read in code with one e2e test, not run here). With Cache Components each slot level keeps up to 3 trees, hidden with <Activity mode="hidden">; otherwise 1 (N692, N693). Back/forward reads the BFCache with staleness bypassed (N799).

Learning the map. Optimistic routing (default on) predicts the route tree for unseen URLs from learned patterns (N659) and refuses interceptable ones (N660; segment-cache/optimistic-routes.ts:1-44, 760-784). Measured: once the client had /sec0/a/1's tree, router.prefetch('/sec0/a/2') sent only the 4,942-B page segment, no /_tree (N1296). The Pages Router's upfront map is §10's contrast. Scale of the code: segment-cache/cache.ts is 4,144 lines and scheduler.ts 2,845 (N809).

Owned elsewhere: the scheduler, prefetch requests, inlining and App Shells (§09); server-side partial rendering (§06).

sections.title: What a visible link costs
figures: fig-prefetch-scheduler · swimlane plus matrix (SVG with an HTML table below) · top: IntersectionObserver (rootMargin 200px) -> microtask batch -> one min-heap ordered priority > phase > recency -> 4 in flight (12 for the hovered link) -> RouteTree / Shell / Speculative phases; hover promotes, scrolling away cancels the queued task but not a fetch in flight; bottom matrix: rows prefetch={false} / default / {true}, columns no Cache Components static, no CC dynamic without loading.tsx, no CC dynamic with loading.tsx, CC, CC + partialPrefetching; each cell gives the strategy and the measured bytes where known ('—' where not) · data: FIG-10; X113, X114; N724-N750; H19, H23-H25

fig-inlining-tradeoff · hint chain plus bars (SVG) · left: the hint chain (root):64 > sec0:96 > guide:96 > g1:96 > __PAGE__:160 with a cut where v2's 4.4 KB-gzip layout fails the < 2,048 B test; right: wire-byte bars for the 12-link page under v0 defaults, v1 inlining off, v2 outlined layout, v5 forced inline, with request counts 24 / 53 / 25 / 24; bottom strip: duplication heatmap, 12 links x (root, sec0, guide), near solid for v0 and one cell per layout for v1 · data: FIG-9; X40; N1311-N1333; H18, H21, H22; lab:scripts/e7-nav.mjs, e7-hints.mjs
sections.brief:
Thesis. What one visible link costs is set by things the build recorded: per-segment prefetch support, inlining hints, loading boundaries and, under Cache Components with partialPrefetching, one App Shell per route. The trade is requests against bytes, and the defaults sit at a defensible point in it.

The scheduler. One IntersectionObserver with a 200px margin watches every prefetchable <Link> (N743; client/components/links.ts:108-127). Tasks sit in one min-heap ordered by priority (Intent 2 > Default 1 > Background 0), then phase (RouteTree > Shell > Speculative), then recency (N724, N725; segment-cache/scheduler.ts:2695-2716). Excerpt X113: segment-cache/scheduler.ts:512-526 (the 4 / 12 cap and its comment "because we don't abort in-progress requests"; N726). Leaving the viewport cancels the queued task, never a fetch in flight (N745). The prefetch prop maps false -> none, true -> full, else auto (N749, N750; client/app-dir/link.tsx:808-827).

One link. Two GETs to the page URL: /_tree (110-282 B decoded) and one page segment (3.9-5.5 KB) with the layouts inlined; a 12-link page cost 24 requests, about 60 KB decoded and 20 KB on the wire (H19, H20; e3-nav.mjs). Segment prefetches never render: the handler answers from the stored segment map with x-nextjs-postponed: 2, or 404s; inlined paths such as /sec0 returned an empty 404 with s-maxage=31536000 (N1294, N1295; build/templates/app-page-runtime.ts:2066-2121). Chunk preloading during prefetch is §10's.

Inlining vs deduplication (C2). The 16.0 post said a shared layout downloads once, "50 links -> once" (N628); 16.2 added prefetchInlining and 16.3 made it a default size heuristic (N1112, N1113). At 16.4 the build gzips each segment's would-be response and offers a parent under 2,048 B gzip to its first child that can take it within a 10,240 B gzip bundle. Excerpt X40: server/app-render/collect-segment-data.tsx:618-624 and 792-800 (two short blocks; N1315, N1316; gzip bytes, V2). Bits: 64 InlinedIntoChild, 32 ParentInlinedIntoSelf, 128 HeadInlinedIntoSelf (N1312). The N=400 prefetch-hints.json is 168,796 B for 401 routes, every layout inlined (H18). Measured on the 12-link page (H21, LOCKED, e7-nav.mjs), requests, decoded / wire bytes: v0 defaults 24, 59,998 / 20,071; v1 inlining off 53, 41,754 / 20,860 (-30% decoded, +3.9% wire); v2 a 4.4 KB-gzip layout outlined and fetched once, 25, 43,964 / 17,235 (cheapest); v5 maxSize 8,192 forcing it inline, 24, 102,179 / 53,941. Root layout in 12 of 12 page responses (H22). Quote prefetchInlining.mdx:13: "at the cost of duplicating some shared segment data across routes".

Partial Prefetching. A default link stops after the Shell phase and fetches one App Shell per route, keyed with every non-root param Fallback (N733, N704; scheduler.ts:2676-2687). Measured (H23, H25): five links to /sec0/a/[id] -> 1 shell request; hub 15 requests, 25,704 / 9,016 B vs 21, 45,334 / 15,195 (-41% wire); the click to /sec0/a/3 then needed one 1,698-B request; the cookies() page got a runtime shell (next-router-prefetch: 3) and its click needed zero.

Without Cache Components, loading.tsx is the cut (N419; create-component-tree.tsx:553-598). A /dyn link still cost a /_tree (178 B) and a metadata-only request (548-550 B), both no-store; with loading.tsx the second became a loading-boundary prefetch and the click payload fell 388 B decoded (H24). Interception (C6): no segment prefetch without CC, for structural reasons (N1361); Chromium's ERR_ABORTED rows were not aborts: 50 reported, all read in full (H30; e7-abort.mjs). With CC the route was prefetched through shells (N1345).

Owned elsewhere: chunk downloads (§10); configuration (§13); cache keys (§08).

sections.title: What each route ships
figures: fig-what-ships · heatmap plus two timelines (SVG) · rows: six placements of one 113 KB client dependency (v0 unused, v1 leaf import, v2 section layout, v3 client next/dynamic on click, v4 next/dynamic from a Server Component, v5 two leaves) x two bundlers; columns: the 53 prerendered pages grouped by section; fill = dependency in first-load JS; hatching = downloaded by prefetch on a page that links there; below, /sec0/p0 -> /sec0/p1 with prefetch on (55.8 KB-gzip chunk fetched on idle, click 0 requests) vs prefetch blocked (click: 1,604 B RSC, then 55,806 B JS) · data: FIG-14; H42, H43; N1372-N1393; lab:scripts/e9-gen-split.mjs, e9-measure.mjs, e9-nav.mjs

fig-route-map-scale · line chart plus stacked bar (SVG) · panel 1: Pages _buildManifest.js raw and gzip bytes at 101 / 401 / 1,001 routes against App's 488 B file loaded by 0 pages; panel 2: first-load JS of /sec0/a/1, Pages vs App, crossover shaded near 490 routes raw / 600 gzip; stacked bar: the 1,001-route manifest by part (bootstrap params 54%, page -> chunk lists, sortedPages, rest); inset: client route resolution us vs dynamic pages scanned (128 -> 1,781 -> 5,148) against the server's 6 / 85 us · data: FIG-17; H44-H49; N1395-N1427; lab:scripts/e9-measure.mjs, e9-resolve.mjs
sections.brief:
Thesis. Per-route splitting means per-route chunk lists and first-load sets, not per-route files. A dependency stays route-scoped in first load, but prefetch spreads its download to every page that links to the route. The Pages Router's upfront route map is the cost the App Router avoids; below a few hundred routes Pages is still cheaper.

How routes get their code. webpack: the server compile creates one client entry per user segment file, containing only the client modules reachable from it (N289, N290; build/webpack/plugins/flight-client-entry-plugin.ts:341-436, 893-948). Turbopack: client chunk groups are chained down the server-component walk, and each layout's group becomes the availability baseline for the segments after it (N1366, N293; crates/next-core/src/next_app/app_client_references_chunks.rs:258-294). A route's first load is the union of its segments' entryJSFiles plus rootMainFiles (N1367; build/route-bundle-stats.ts:155-175); for Turbopack App routes it equalled the HTML's script tags minus the noModule polyfill exactly (N1381). Physical files follow chunker thresholds: minChunkSize 50,000 B, maxMergeChunkSize 200,000 B (N872; turbopackChunking.mdx § Size Thresholds).

Tiny pages (H12-H14, measure-dist.mjs): Turbopack emitted the same 10 client chunks (591 KB) at 21, 101 and 401 routes; webpack 47, 143, 503. First loads 463,623 / 464,045 / 464,348 B; the 422-B SectionNav chunk separates /sec0/a/[id] from /dyn.

A real dependency (H42; synthetic, gzips only 2.0x): leaf import -> 1 of 53 pages (+112,993 B); section-layout import -> all 19 pages of that section; two leaves -> one shared chunk; next/dynamic from a Server Component did not split (+3,260 B over a plain import), as the docs warn (lazy-loading.mdx:60); only a client-side next/dynamic rendered on click kept it out of every first load.

Prefetch carries code. Excerpt X131: compiled/react-server-dom-turbopack/cjs/react-server-dom-turbopack-client.browser.production.js:86-92, preloadModule loading every chunk an import row names (verbatim; N1369). Measured (H43, e9-nav.mjs): a page that only linked to the heavy route downloaded its 55,806-B chunk during idle prefetch; with the import in a layout, a page in another section downloaded it, because its header linked into that section and the prefetched segment inlined the layout's script reference; blocking prefetch moved the download to the click as a waterfall, 1,604 B RSC then 55,806 B JS. The plain app showed the same with a 302-B Counter chunk (N1393).

The Pages contrast. Every Pages page loads _buildManifest.js: sortedPages, per-page chunks and, under Turbopack, per-page bootstrap params (N1028, N1397). It grew from 18,590 B (3,988 gzip) at 101 routes to 73,527 (14,424) at 401 and 183,519 (34,623) at 1,001, about 183 B raw per route, 54% of it bootstrap params at 1,001 (N1395, N1396). Pages first load for /sec0/a/1 went 389,116 -> 563,131 B (route map 5.1% -> 34.4%); App stayed 464,039 -> 464,709 B; the crossover is near 490 routes raw or 600 gzip, by interpolation (H45). route-bundle-stats omits the Pages route map (N1405). Client resolution compiles a regex per dynamic page per call (N1424; shared/lib/router/router.ts:204-221): 128 us at 28 dynamic pages, 1,781 us at 298, against the server's 6 / 85 us (H48). The Pages twin built at 0.58-0.65x the App app's CPU-seconds (H46). Bloom filters cost only Pages pages of mixed apps: +3,505 B raw (H49). Quote the Layouts RFC (23 May 2022, § Server-Centric Routing): client-side routing "scales poorly when the number of potential routes is large because the client has to download a route map" (N1081).

Owned elsewhere: "use client" placement (§13); prefetch scheduling (§09); placement practices (§13).

sections.title: Why it is efficient, and what it costs
figures: fig-price-ledger · stack rows (HTML) · one row per precomputation the tree enables (discovery once; routing as table lookups; rendering below shared layouts; per-route client code; per-URL prerender with stored prefetch artifacts; no upfront route map; tree-keyed invalidation), with cells: what the build computes (hl-blue), what it saves, measured (hl-green), what it costs, measured (hl-red), who pays · data: DOSSIER §1.10; H2, H9, H10, H15, H20, H26, H28, H32, H34, H37, H45, H46
sections.brief:
Thesis. The synthesis. The file tree turns runtime questions into build-time facts, which pays off in seven places; each has a measured price, and some prices land on people who did not choose the feature. The judgement is reconstruction: badge it, and tie each number to the section that derived it.

Seven precomputations (DOSSIER §1.10), each with one number. (1) Discovery happens once and private folders are never read (lib/recursive-readdir.ts:81-86; 2.5-5x walk ratio, H50). (2) Routing is table lookups: Set probes for static URLs and a pre-sorted regex scan for dynamic ones (85 us at 1,000 dynamic routes against a 2.37 ms static TTFB; H34, H31). (3) Rendering can start below the shared layouts and the client keeps their state (dynamic navigations 41-52% smaller; layout DOM nodes kept; H28, H26). (4) Each route ships only its segments' client code (113 KB dependency in 1 of 53 first loads; H42). (5) Prerendering is per URL and precomputes prefetch artifacts, so prefetches are answered from stored buffers and never run app code (app-page-runtime.ts:2066-2121; 0-request clicks, H26). (6) The client needs no upfront route map (App first load flat within 0.15% from 101 to 1,001 routes while Pages grew 45%; H45). (7) Invalidation is keyed by the tree (folder-derived soft tags; N567).

The prices, each with its number. Payload twice on a hard load (HTML 1.47-1.73x its RSC, N1210; the leaf boundary case 5.6x RSC and 2.3x HTML, H15). Prefetch traffic grows with links: two requests per visible link, small layouts duplicated on purpose, linked routes' chunks downloaded (H20, H22, H43). Builds pay per page: static generation about 24 s at N=400 whether cold, warm or after one edit, about 60% of a warm build, while compile fell from 25.2 s to 1.86 s (H7, H9). Defaults that hurt small machines: 7 workers on a 2-CPU quota (-21% wall when pinned, H2); a build cache that costs +19% CPU when no CI restores it (H10); preloading that makes the first request after a deploy 1.24 s (H37). Proxy: about 0.9 ms of CPU per matched request, +39% on a static page (H32). Interception adds a Vary dimension and forfeits prefetching without Cache Components (H29). PPR responses stay private, no-store under next start (H35). A route conflict can pass the build and fail at start (H39).

Who pays. Contrast App and Pages on the same app (H44-H47): App HTML about 3x Pages HTML because it inlines the Flight payload (9,954 vs 3,472 B, N1406); App builds cost 1.5-1.7x the CPU (Pages 0.58-0.65x); App first load is flat while Pages grows about 183 B per route and overtakes App near 490 routes. State plainly where the design wins (large route counts, shared layouts, static-heavy sites with many links) and where it does not pay for itself here (small apps, build-time budgets, CDN caching of dynamic pages).

A .measured stat-tile row (4 tiles, not a figure) may lead: 0 requests (prefetched static click), 85 us (1,000 dynamic routes), about 24 s (static generation, every build), 0.9 ms (no-op Proxy).

sections.title: Faster, cheaper builds
figures: fig-build-cost · grouped stacked bars (SVG) · N=400 builds: Turbopack cold QUIET (compile 25.2 s, TypeScript 13.8, static generation 21.7; wall 70.4), warm QUIET (1.86 / 4.9 / 22.2; 38.4), one-file edit (2.0 / 5.7 / 23.5; 41.5), cold with experimental.cpus 2 (23.8 / 13.3 / 14.3; 55.9), cold with the build cache off (20.6 / 9.4 / 21.8; 60.3); webpack cold QUIET (54 / 13.65 / 25.65; 134.3) and warm (28.3 / 4.8 / 25.2; 99.3); phase spans drawn side by side with wall time as a separate tick because spans overlap; inset: max(1, os.cpus().length - 1) = 7 inside a 2-CPU cgroup · data: FIG-16; lab/results/summary-builds.csv (medians, n=3 per cell); H2, H7-H10
sections.brief:
Thesis. A build splits into compilation, which the Turbopack cache makes nearly free, and static generation, which it never skips. On containers the defaults are wrong twice: the worker count and the cache write. next dev measures neither.

Each practice gets mechanism, measured effect and when not to use it (P-ids from DOSSIER §5).

Restore .next/cache, or turn the build cache off (P5). Turbopack persists its task graph to .next/cache/turbopack and the clean step keeps cache/ (build/index.ts:1379-1388). Warm compile fell 13 -> 0.50 s, 15.2 -> 0.69 s and 25.2 -> 1.86 s at 21 / 101 / 401 routes (13.5-26x, H7); a one-file edit rebuilt like a warm build (compile 2.0 s, wall 41.5 vs 40.9 s, H8). Where nothing restores the cache, the write is pure cost: +19% CPU (117.8 vs 99.3 CPU-s with experimental.turbopackFileSystemCacheForBuild: false) and about 10 s of wall at N=400; the turbopack-persistence span alone was 8.1-9.0 s (H10; run-e1bc.sh). The same flag also switches dependency tracking (N816; build/turbopack-build/impl.ts:67-69, 115-118). Docs: turbopackFileSystemCache.mdx § Build environments; ci-build-caching.mdx. When not: never disable it where the cache is restored.

Set experimental.cpus to the container's quota (P6). Excerpt X35: server/config-shared.ts:2422-2426 (verbatim). It counts host CPUs (os.cpus().length, or CIRCLE_NODE_TOTAL). Measured QUIET at N=400 (H2): 7 -> 2 workers took wall 70.4 -> 55.9 s (-21%), CPU 117.8 -> 90.6 CPU-s (-23%), static generation 21.7 -> 14.3 s, summed peak RSS 2.31 -> 1.35 GiB (-41%, which double-counts shared pages); cgroup throttling 49.6 vs 19.4 s (M2). The contended comparison showed -43% and overstates it (H3). When not: only 2 and 7 workers were tested, and staticGenerationMaxConcurrency (8) and staticGenerationMinPagesPerWorker (25) interact (W15); claim only that quota beat the default here.

Prerender only high-value params; treat page count as the warm-build floor (P7). Static generation took 24.7 / 24.2 / 23.5 s cold / warm / edit at N=400 and re-rendered all 756 pages, about 60% of a warm build (H9). Unlisted params render on first request and are cached (/sec0/a/7: MISS, then HIT; N1285, n=1). Docs: incremental-static-regeneration-cache-components.mdx § Choosing what to prerender. When not: top-traffic pages that must be instant on first visit.

Type-check in a parallel CI job (P8). App type-checking is a serial phase after compile (N819); TypeScript took 13.8 s cold and 3.4-5.0 s warm at N=400 (M14). ignoreBuildErrors still validates config (N820); next build no longer lints (N822).

Bundler choice. A cold webpack build used 1.60-1.63x Turbopack's CPU-seconds (H5); webpack's warm compile was 28.3 s against 1.86 s (N1148); webpack alone runs the NFT pass, 20-53 s spans (M15).

Dev. next dev compiles on demand and prefetches nothing (N834, N839). First hit 7.96 s (Turbopack) vs 14.66 s (webpack); second route 1.33 vs 4.96 s (H40). The log line "GET … in 756ms" covered a request the client saw take about 7 s (N1232). Stop dev with Ctrl-C: after SIGINT and 15 s idle a 55 MB cache cut the restart's first hit 7.17 -> 2.01 s; after SIGTERM plus kill there was no gain (H41; the trigger, idle vs signal, is unisolated, C8). --debug-build-paths builds only matching routes (N298, N828). Private folders shorten discovery 2.5-5x (H50), a minor effect.

Owned elsewhere: the worker mechanism (§03); request, bundle and navigation practices (§13).

sections.brief:
Thesis. The request-time and client practices that moved numbers in the lab, each tied to its mechanism and to the case where it does not apply. h3 groups: Proxy and config routes; request APIs and rendering; client boundaries and heavy code; prefetch and navigation; data; serving. Use P-ids (DOSSIER §5), two to four sentences per practice.

Proxy and config routes. Narrow the matcher or remove proxy.ts (P9: +0.93 ms p50 per matched request, H32); write '/about/:path*', not '/about', because the matcher is end-anchored (N364); excluding a page also excludes its Server Functions (N376). Prefer next.config redirects, rewrites and headers for static rules, compiled once into the phase list (P10; server/lib/router-utils/filesystem.ts:137-170).

Request APIs and rendering. Legacy model: keep cookies() and headers() out of shared and root layouts, because one call makes the whole route dynamic and no-store (P11; 5.55 vs 2.37 ms TTFB p50, H31; N886). Cache Components: push request reads below a <Suspense> and pass promises instead of awaiting at the top (P12; N891, N507); PPR /dyn TTFB 3.63 vs 6.45 ms, but private, no-store, 1.9x later and 1.9x the bytes (H35). Use generateStaticParams for prerenderable dynamic routes (P22; 2.63 ms, HIT).

Client boundaries and heavy code. Place "use client" deliberately (P18): the docs' leaf rule (server-and-client-components.mdx § Reducing JS bundle size, N846) holds for interactive leaves, but in E2 moving the boundary up to a layout wrapper added 38,489 B raw (6,303 gzip) of JS to every route while cutting RSC 82% and HTML 56%, because a 400-item server-rendered list is serialized into Flight and inlined again (H15, C7). Weigh code size against rendered-output size. Keep heavy libraries behind a client-side next/dynamic rendered on interaction (P19) and import shared widgets in leaves, not layouts (P20); a Server Component next/dynamic does not split (H42).

Prefetch and navigation. Leave prefetchInlining on (P14: 20,071 vs 20,860 B wire against inlining-off, with 24 vs 53 requests; raising maxSize tripled bytes, H21). Adopt Cache Components with partialPrefetching when many links share a pattern (P13: -41% prefetch wire on the hub; one request at the click, H23). Without Cache Components add loading.tsx to dynamic routes for instant fallback UI, not free prefetches (P15, H24). Use prefetch={false} or hover-only on long lists of links to dynamic, cookie-reading or heavy routes (P16; in the App Router false disables hover too, N966); avoid prefetch={true} on cookie-reading routes without CC (P17; client/app-dir/link.tsx:808-827). Use interception only where the modal is worth a Vary dimension (P23).

Data. Keep layouts stable and data-light; refetch in children and rely on per-request fetch and React.cache dedupe (P21; server/lib/dedupe-fetch.ts:44-89; N883). Do not await in sequence what can start together (N876) or call your own Route Handler from a Server Component (N882).

Serving. Decide preloadEntriesOnStart by traffic (P27: 1.24 s vs 394 ms first request; keep it where servers idle first, 146 vs 205 ms). Multi-instance self-hosting needs cacheHandler with cacheMaxMemorySize: 0, and cacheHandlers (P26). Behind a CDN preserve rsc, _rsc and Vary (P28); revalidatePath does not purge a CDN (P25). Load fonts and scripts in the layout that needs them (P24).

Figure caption: "high boundary: more JS, much smaller payload; leaf: less JS, payload shipped twice", the lab caveat, and that summed script tags (576,708 B) include the 112,594-B noModule polyfill (H14).

sections.brief:
Thesis. The beliefs the code or the lab contradicts at 16.4, and the anti-patterns they lead to. A reference section: one belief, one correction, one source, and a pointer to the section that explains it (§NN). Do not re-derive mechanisms.

Myths for the table (pick about fourteen; corrected wording):
- "Next scans app/ on each request": manifests are read once at boot; Set probes and a sorted regex scan (N327, N329; §05).
- "Every file in app/ becomes a route": only page, route and metadata files do (N6; §02).
- "proxy.ts is middleware.ts renamed": Proxy always compiles for Node.js and rejects runtime config; middleware.ts still targets edge (N112, N113; §02).
- "A matcher '/about' also covers /about/team": the compiled regex is end-anchored (N364, measured; proxy.mdx § Matcher says otherwise; §05).
- "A soft navigation fetches only the changed segment": true for dynamic targets only (C3; §06).
- "Next 16 downloads a shared layout once for all links": with default inlining small layouts ride in every page prefetch, 12 of 12 (C2, H22; §09).
- "A dynamic route without loading.tsx is not prefetched": no segment data, but /_tree plus a metadata-only request per link, both no-store (H24; §09).
- "Intercepted-route prefetches are aborted by the client": the client never aborts; Chromium mislabels fully read dynamic gzip responses (C6, H30; §09).
- "Server Components ship no JavaScript, so always push 'use client' to the leaves": rendered output ships twice (C7, H15; §13).
- "Code splitting means a heavy component costs only its page": prefetch preloads linked routes' chunks (H43; §10).
- "The Turbopack cache makes builds fast": it makes compilation fast; static generation is untouched and the write costs +19% CPU when nothing restores it (H7, H9, H10; §12).
- "next build uses the CPUs you give it": it sizes workers from os.cpus(), 7 inside a 2-CPU cgroup (H1; §03).
- "Cache Components is on by default in 16.4": only in new create-next-app projects; the framework default is false (N466, N1120; §07).
- "PPR pages are CDN-cacheable out of the box": a postponed route is sent private, no-store under next start (N607; §07).
- "next build catches every route conflict": /[a]/x plus /[b]/y builds and crashes next start (H39; §03).
- "Prefetching works in next dev": dev prefetches nothing, and its log line omitted a 7 s compile (N839, N1232; §12).
- "Scrolling a link away cancels its prefetch": it cancels the queued task, not the fetch (N745; §09).

Prose (about 450 words) groups the anti-patterns: analytics or auth checks in a layout body (runs on prefetch, N919; not re-run on navigation, N428); conditional slots expected to save work (both render, N74); a request API in the root layout under the legacy model (the whole app goes dynamic, N886); raising maxSize to save requests (H21); sibling dynamic folders with different param names (H39); a matcher-less proxy.ts (runs on _next/static, N116); measuring with next dev or by summing <script> tags (112,594-B polyfill, H14).

Close with the docs-vs-code list from W12, one line each, code wins: matcher anchoring; the three default.js answers; strict matching's undocumented opt-out; the Link scroll algorithm (layout-router.tsx:55-116, 144-278); "Cache-Control: public" in self-hosting.mdx vs cache-control.ts:30-34; the "use cache" timeout, 54 s in code (config.ts:1793-1799) vs 50 s in use-cache.mdx (N536).
